clinicalPearls: Presents with a variable combination of third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerve palsies with sensory disturbance in the first and often second trigeminal divisions
A Horner syndrome may coexist with a sixth nerve palsy because the sympathetic fibres briefly travel with the abducens nerve within the sinus
The sixth nerve lies free within the sinus and is often affected early, while the other motor nerves run in the lateral wall
Vision is usually preserved unless the lesion extends anteriorly to the orbital apex to involve the optic nerve
Proptosis, chemosis, and an audible bruit suggest a carotid-cavernous fistula
Causes include tumour, aneurysm of the intracavernous carotid, thrombosis, fistula, and inflammatory or infective disease
Bilateral involvement can occur because the two cavernous sinuses communicate across the midline
reference.pathophysiology: The cavernous sinus is a venous channel flanking the sphenoid sinus and pituitary that transmits the intracavernous internal carotid artery and its surrounding sympathetic plexus, the abducens nerve within its lumen, and the oculomotor, trochlear, and ophthalmic (and often maxillary) trigeminal nerves in its lateral wall. Lesions here produce painful or painless ophthalmoplegia with trigeminal sensory loss, and the proximity of sympathetic fibres to the abducens nerve can yield a combined sixth nerve palsy and Horner syndrome. Responsible processes include neoplasm, intracavernous aneurysm, septic and aseptic thrombosis, carotid-cavernous fistula, and granulomatous inflammation.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital apex syndrome with optic nerve involvement
Skull base metastasis or nasopharyngeal carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and cavernous sinus with contrast
Magnetic resonance or CT angiography and venography to assess the carotid, aneurysm, fistula, or thrombosis
Endocrine assessment when a pituitary lesion is suspected
Screening for malignancy and nasopharyngeal disease
Catheter angiography where a fistula or aneurysm requires definition
redFlags: Features of cavernous sinus thrombosis such as fever, proptosis, and rapid bilateral progression
Proptosis with a bruit suggesting a high-flow carotid-cavernous fistula
Acute severe headache with visual loss suggesting pituitary apoplexy or aneurysm
Rapidly progressive multiple cranial neuropathies suggesting malignant infiltration
reference.prognosis: Outcome is determined by the cause; thrombosis and fistulae can be managed with good results if treated promptly, while malignant infiltration carries a poorer prognosis, and residual ophthalmoplegia may persist after resolution.
pitfalls: Overlooking a coexisting Horner syndrome that localises the lesion to the cavernous sinus
Missing a carotid-cavernous fistula by not examining for proptosis and bruit
Failing to exclude an intracavernous aneurysm before assuming inflammation
Not recognising the possibility of bilateral spread through the intercavernous connections
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Cause-directed therapy is the mainstay: tumour-directed surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, and endovascular treatment of a carotid-cavernous fistula or intracavernous aneurysm
Broad-spectrum antibiotics with source control of contiguous sinusitis, and anticoagulation, for septic cavernous sinus thrombosis
Corticosteroids for granulomatous or idiopathic inflammatory (Tolosa-Hunt) disease
Analgesia and symptomatic care for painful ophthalmoplegia
Ocular protection with lubrication and treatment of exposure, plus prisms or occlusion for diplopia
Multidisciplinary care across neurology, ophthalmology, neurosurgery, interventional radiology, ENT and oncology
Serial neuro-ophthalmic monitoring of cranial nerve function and vision, escalating for anterior extension threatening the optic nerve
